title: 11-Year-Old Bodhana Makes Chess History
summary:
Imagine becoming one of the world's top chess players before finishing middle school! For Bodhana Sivanandan, an 11-year-old from northwest London, England, this is already a reality. On September 26, 2026, she became the youngest person ever to earn the Woman Grandmaster title. The record was previously held by Kateryna Lagno, who was 12 when she won it in 2002.

The Woman Grandmaster title is one of the highest honors in chess. To earn it, a player must reach a rating of at least 2,300 points through strong performances in official matches, and meet certain requirements in three qualifying tournaments to achieve what are called norms.

Bodhana's journey began during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, when she was five years old. A friend of her father gave the family a bag of toys and books. Inside, Bodhana discovered a chessboard and became curious about the game. Her father encouraged her to learn, and she quickly developed a passion for it.

Her talent showed early. At age seven, she won all 24 of her games at the European Schools Championship, earning three gold medals. Two years later, she was selected to represent England at the 2024 Chess Olympiad in Hungary, the youngest person ever to compete for England in any international sporting competition. In 2025, at just 10 years old, she became the youngest girl to beat a Grandmaster, Peter Wells, in a classical game at the British Chess Championships.

In August 2026, she became the youngest-ever British women's chess champion. The following month, at the 46th Chess Olympiad in Samarkand as England's top player, she played all 11 rounds of the tournament, winning six games, drawing four, and losing just one. That performance earned her the third and final norm, completing her record-breaking title. Bodhana hopes to eventually earn the Grandmaster title, which is open to players of any gender. When not playing chess, she is a regular middle school student who enjoys playing the piano and violin, as well as reading.
why_it_matters: Bodhana's record shows how far young talent can go with early encouragement and steady practice, and it may inspire more young players, especially girls, to take up competitive chess.
